questions.stem: This four-panel sequence shows dual pathways within the AV node, a premature beat, retrograde conduction, and an established loop. What arrhythmia mechanism is depicted?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Complete AV block with a ventricular escape rhythm

choices.label: D
choices.text: Enhanced automaticity of an ectopic atrial focus

explanation.summary: AVNRT arises when a premature impulse blocks in the fast pathway, travels down the slow pathway, then conducts retrogradely up the fast pathway, creating a self-sustaining reentrant loop within the AV node.
explanation.whyCorrect: AVNRT arises when a premature impulse blocks in the fast pathway, travels down the slow pathway, then conducts retrogradely up the fast pathway, creating a self-sustaining reentrant loop within the AV node.

questions.stem: This four-chamber diagram highlights an abnormal muscular bridge (green) directly connecting the right atrium to the right ventricle, bypassing the AV node. What is this structure and its consequence?

choices.label: A
choices.text: An accessory pathway causing ventricular pre-excitation

choices.label: B
choices.text: A normal moderator band conducting to the RV apex

choices.label: C
choices.text: A dilated coronary sinus draining the myocardium

choices.label: D
choices.text: An enlarged AV node causing first-degree block

choices.label: E
choices.text: A patent foramen ovale allowing atrial shunting

explanation.summary: An accessory AV connection lets atrial impulses reach the ventricle before the AV-node delay, pre-exciting the ventricle (delta wave) and providing a limb for reentrant tachycardia in WPW.
explanation.whyCorrect: An accessory AV connection lets atrial impulses reach the ventricle before the AV-node delay, pre-exciting the ventricle (delta wave) and providing a limb for reentrant tachycardia in WPW.

questions.stem: This diagram classifies arrhythmias by their site of origin above versus below the AV junction. On the surface ECG, what typically distinguishes an arrhythmia arising from the upper (supraventricular) site?

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prolonged PR interval as a defining feature

choices.label: C
choices.text: A wide QRS complex from slow myocyte-to-myocyte spread

choices.label: E
choices.text: Absence of any P waves in every case

explanation.summary: Supraventricular impulses still descend the normal conduction system, so ventricular depolarization is rapid and the QRS stays narrow; ventricular-origin arrhythmias spread cell-to-cell and produce a wide QRS.
explanation.whyCorrect: Supraventricular impulses still descend the normal conduction system, so ventricular depolarization is rapid and the QRS stays narrow; ventricular-origin arrhythmias spread cell-to-cell and produce a wide QRS.

questions.stem: This ventricular cardiac action potential shows a long refractory period spanning depolarization through most of repolarization. What is the functional significance of this prolonged refractory period?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It sets the resting membrane potential during phase 4

choices.label: B
choices.text: It prevents tetanic contraction and re-excitation

choices.label: C
choices.text: It allows rapid repetitive firing to increase force by summation

choices.label: D
choices.text: It triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum

choices.label: E
choices.text: It generates the pacemaker funny current in the SA node

explanation.summary: Because Na+ channels stay inactivated through the plateau, cardiac muscle cannot be re-stimulated until it has largely repolarized. This long refractory period blocks tetany and premature reentry, protecting diastolic filling.
explanation.whyCorrect: Because Na+ channels stay inactivated through the plateau, cardiac muscle cannot be re-stimulated until it has largely repolarized. This long refractory period blocks tetany and premature reentry, protecting diastolic filling.

questions.stem: The table pairs conduction system components with their intrinsic firing rates, which decrease from the SA node down to the Purkinje fibers. What is the physiological consequence of this gradient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The SA node normally drives the heart

choices.label: B
choices.text: Distal pacemakers speed up the heart during exercise

choices.label: C
choices.text: The AV node is the fastest and dominant pacemaker

choices.label: D
choices.text: All pacemakers fire simultaneously to summate the rate

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Purkinje fibers set heart rate because they fire last

explanation.summary: The fastest pacemaker sets the rhythm and resets slower sites before they reach threshold (overdrive suppression). If the SA node fails, a subsidiary pacemaker with its slower intrinsic rate takes over as an escape rhythm.
explanation.whyCorrect: The fastest pacemaker sets the rhythm and resets slower sites before they reach threshold (overdrive suppression). If the SA node fails, a subsidiary pacemaker with its slower intrinsic rate takes over as an escape rhythm.

questions.stem: The upper tracing shows an oscillation interrupting the plateau/repolarization; the lower shows one after the cell has returned toward rest. Which arrhythmia is classically caused by the upper (early afterdepolarization) mechanism?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Torsades de pointes in the setting of QT prolongation

choices.label: B
choices.text: First-degree AV block from nodal delay

choices.label: C
choices.text: Wolff-Parkinson-White reentry via an accessory pathway

choices.label: E
choices.text: Atrial fibrillation from pulmonary vein reentry

explanation.summary: Early afterdepolarizations arise during phases 2-3 when repolarization is prolonged (long QT), reactivating inward currents. They can trigger torsades de pointes; delayed afterdepolarizations (lower tracing) relate to calcium overload, e.g., digoxin toxicity.
explanation.whyCorrect: Early afterdepolarizations arise during phases 2-3 when repolarization is prolonged (long QT), reactivating inward currents. They can trigger torsades de pointes; delayed afterdepolarizations (lower tracing) relate to calcium overload, e.g., digoxin toxicity.

questions.stem: This rhythm strip shows a wide-complex tachycardia whose QRS amplitude progressively waxes and wanes, appearing to twist around the baseline. In a patient on a QT-prolonging Class IA antiarrhythmic, what is this rhythm?

explanation.summary: The characteristic twisting of QRS amplitude around the baseline is torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with QT prolongation. Class IA agents (and other QT-prolonging drugs) can precipitate it.
explanation.whyCorrect: The characteristic twisting of QRS amplitude around the baseline is torsades de pointes, a polymorphic ventricular tachycardia associated with QT prolongation. Class IA agents (and other QT-prolonging drugs) can precipitate it.

questions.stem: This overlay compares a normal cardiac action potential (black) with one altered by a drug (red): phase 0 is minimally changed while the action potential duration is shortened. A drug producing this pattern is best exemplified by which agent?

explanation.summary: The pattern (weak Na+ channel block with shortened action potential duration) is characteristic of Class IB agents such as lidocaine and mexiletine, which preferentially act on ischemic/depolarized ventricular tissue. Quinidine is IA, flecainide is IC, amiodarone is III, verapamil is IV.
explanation.whyCorrect: The pattern (weak Na+ channel block with shortened action potential duration) is characteristic of Class IB agents such as lidocaine and mexiletine, which preferentially act on ischemic/depolarized ventricular tissue. Quinidine is IA, flecainide is IC, amiodarone is III, verapamil is IV.

questions.stem: This overlay compares a normal action potential (black) with one altered by a drug (red): the phase 0 upstroke slope is markedly reduced while the overall action potential duration is essentially unchanged. Which agent typifies this effect?

explanation.summary: Marked slowing of phase 0 (strong Na+ channel block) with little change in action potential duration is the hallmark of Class IC agents such as flecainide and propafenone. Lidocaine is IB (shortens APD), quinidine is IA (prolongs APD), sotalol is III, diltiazem is IV.
explanation.whyCorrect: Marked slowing of phase 0 (strong Na+ channel block) with little change in action potential duration is the hallmark of Class IC agents such as flecainide and propafenone. Lidocaine is IB (shortens APD), quinidine is IA (prolongs APD), sotalol is III, diltiazem is IV.

questions.stem: This overlay compares a normal action potential (black) with one altered by a drug (red): the phase 0 slope is reduced AND repolarization is prolonged, increasing action potential duration and effective refractory period. Which agent produces this combined effect?

explanation.summary: Combined moderate Na+ channel block (slowed phase 0) plus K+ channel block (prolonged repolarization, increased APD/ERP) is characteristic of Class IA agents such as quinidine, procainamide, and disopyramide. This QT prolongation predisposes to torsades de pointes.
explanation.whyCorrect: Combined moderate Na+ channel block (slowed phase 0) plus K+ channel block (prolonged repolarization, increased APD/ERP) is characteristic of Class IA agents such as quinidine, procainamide, and disopyramide. This QT prolongation predisposes to torsades de pointes.

questions.stem: This ventricular cardiac action potential is annotated with its phases and the corresponding transmembrane ion movements shown below. What ionic mechanism produces the sustained plateau (phase 2)?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Activity of the Na+/K+-ATPase pumping Na+ inward

choices.label: D
choices.text: Inward Ca2+ current balanced by outward K+ current

choices.label: E
choices.text: Outward K+ current with no inward current

explanation.summary: Phase 2 (plateau) results from a balance between inward Ca2+ current (through L-type channels) and outward K+ current. Phase 0 is the rapid Na+ influx, and phase 3 repolarization is dominated by K+ efflux once Ca2+ channels close.
explanation.whyCorrect: Phase 2 (plateau) results from a balance between inward Ca2+ current (through L-type channels) and outward K+ current. Phase 0 is the rapid Na+ influx, and phase 3 repolarization is dominated by K+ efflux once Ca2+ channels close.

questions.stem: This diagram depicts a voltage-gated sodium channel cycling through three conformations, with an activation gate and an inactivation gate labeled. In the resting state (left panel), what is the configuration of the two gates?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Activation gate open, inactivation gate open

choices.label: B
choices.text: Activation gate open, inactivation gate closed

choices.label: C
choices.text: Both gates fused into a single open pore

choices.label: D
choices.text: Activation gate closed, inactivation gate open

choices.label: E
choices.text: Activation gate closed, inactivation gate closed

explanation.summary: At rest, the activation gate is closed and the inactivation gate is open, so no Na+ flows. On depolarization the activation gate opens (activated state, Na+ flows), then the inactivation gate closes (inactivated state). Class I drugs bind preferentially to the activated/inactivated states.
explanation.whyCorrect: At rest, the activation gate is closed and the inactivation gate is open, so no Na+ flows. On depolarization the activation gate opens (activated state, Na+ flows), then the inactivation gate closes (inactivated state). Class I drugs bind preferentially to the activated/inactivated states.

questions.stem: This ECG shows narrow QRS complexes with no discernible P waves before them at a regular, slow rate. What rhythm is this?

explanation.summary: When the SA node fails, an AV-junctional pacemaker takes over. Because the impulse originates near the AV node, the QRS stays narrow but P waves are absent or buried, producing a junctional escape rhythm.
explanation.whyCorrect: When the SA node fails, an AV-junctional pacemaker takes over. Because the impulse originates near the AV node, the QRS stays narrow but P waves are absent or buried, producing a junctional escape rhythm.

questions.stem: This 12-lead ECG shows a regular rhythm with an upright P wave preceding each narrow QRS complex. What is the underlying rhythm?

explanation.summary: A consistent P wave before every narrow QRS at a regular interval indicates that the SA node is pacing and conduction is intact, the definition of normal sinus rhythm.
explanation.whyCorrect: A consistent P wave before every narrow QRS at a regular interval indicates that the SA node is pacing and conduction is intact, the definition of normal sinus rhythm.

questions.stem: On this rhythm strip a normal complex is followed by a flat line of two or more seconds before the next beat. This absence of electrical activity reflects failure of which structure?

explanation.summary: A sinus pause occurs when the SA node transiently fails to depolarize, producing a flat baseline with no P-QRS-T until sinus activity resumes or an escape beat intervenes.
explanation.whyCorrect: A sinus pause occurs when the SA node transiently fails to depolarize, producing a flat baseline with no P-QRS-T until sinus activity resumes or an escape beat intervenes.
